body_markdown:
“You eat one lousy foot and they call you a cannibal. What a world.”


With that, washed-up busman Dan Torrance seems to be at his end. But it is only the beginning. Everyone remembers *Airplane!* , the hilariously quotable 1980 sendup of Hollywood disaster flicks that launched a whole genre of movies serving slapstick on a conveyor belt. Today it’s considered a work of comedic genius. And yet, in certain moments, *Airplane!* looks like a shot-for-shot remake of *The Big Bus* , which appeared four years earlier and which hardly anyone remembers.


*Welcome to the[Hagerty Movies and Cars Celebration](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/welcome-to-the-hagerty-movies-and-cars-celebration/) , where we highlight and explore the relationship between[cars and the silver screen](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/movies-and-cars/) .*


Movies are all about the metaphor, and in the early ’70s, the time was apparently ripe for films in which inflation, the energy crisis, the pollution crisis, Watergate, and the demise of convertibles in favor of vinyl landau tops got translated onscreen as so many crashing airplanes, burning skyscrapers, capsizing ocean liners, and city-shaking temblors. The hackneyed formula—an ensemble cast of Hollywood B-listers playing hysterical schlubs with melodramatic backstories clawing their way through one climactic set piece after another—was made for parody. *Airplane!* gets credit for doing it the best, but *The Big Bus* did it first.


Paramount Pictures


In case you missed it—or, more likely, were high when you saw it— *The Big Bus* follows the star-crossed journey of the nuclear-powered, double-decked Cyclops as it attempts to set a nonstop record from New York to, ahem, Denver (both of which look suspiciously like the mountains around Los Angeles). Dark forces conspire against it on behalf of oil sheiks who fear the replacement of fossil fuels with nukes. The cast was suitably ensembley, with Lynn Redgrave, Ned Beatty, Larry Hagman, Stockard Channing, Ruth Gordon, José Ferrer, *WKRP’s* Howard Hesseman, Sally Kellerman, and *Rockford Files’* Stuart Margolin all riding the crazy bus. It wasn’t an easy shoot: Channing’s character, Kitty Baxter, at one point backstrokes through a flood of soda pop pumped into the galley to keep the Cyclops from going over a cliff.


Paramount Pictures


As with *Airplane!* , the movie works (sort of) because the cast is full-send, playing out the batty screenplay with faces as straight as a Nebraska interstate. But 50 years on, the signature achievement of *The Big Bus* is arguably the Cyclops itself, a 110-foot-long, 32-wheel, 65-mph full-scale bus built by Paramount’s Construction and Special Effects Department. As in the movie, it had dual working controls and was piloted by costumed stunt drivers communicating through headsets. The cockpit and the upstairs piano lounge were the only finished bits of the interior, the rest being running gear and empty space. The onboard bowling alley and swimming pool were soundstage sets (all that plus the lounge, the kitchen, a private dining room, and seats for 180 passengers fitting into the bus is one of the quiet jokes of the movie).


The first appearance of the Cyclops in the film is appropriately grandiose, the mega-bus being pulled from its hangar to the thundering tones of Strauss’ *Also sprach Zarathustra.* It remains the second and second-best cinematic use of that piece after *2001: A Space Odyssey.* Nowadays, when anything larger than a Toyota Corolla is faked in CGI, the Cyclops fully earns its bombastic entrance as one of the greatest roadgoing, in-real-life vehicle props ever constructed, a relic from a bygone era when the big studios built big things to fill big screens. Even for dumb movies.
